claim: Cycling of co-substrates, whereby a metabolite is converted among alternate forms via different reactions, is ubiquitous in metabolism.
source: Cycling of co-substrates, whereby a metabolite is converted among alternate forms via different reactions, is ubiquitous in metabolism.
evidence: This is a general statement about metabolism presented in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Several cycled co-substrates are well known as energy and electron carriers (e.g. ATP and NAD(P)H).
source: Several cycled co-substrates are well known as energy and electron carriers (e.g. ATP and NAD(P)H), but there are also other metabolites that act as cycled co-substrates in different parts of central metabolism.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the roles of ATP and NAD(P)H in metabolism.

claim: Co-substrate cycling imposes an additional flux limit on a reaction, distinct to the limit imposed by the kinetics of the primary enzyme catalysing that reaction.
source: In the cases of a single reaction and linear pathways, we find that co-substrate cycling imposes an additional flux limit on a reaction, distinct to the limit imposed by the kinetics of the primary enzyme catalysing that reaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical analysis and analytical methods presented in the manuscript.

claim: The additional flux limit imposed by co-substrate cycling is a function of the total pool size and turnover rate of the cycled co-substrate.
source: Using analytical methods, we show that this additional limit is a function of the total pool size and turnover rate of the cycled co-substrate.
evidence: This is derived analytically from the mathematical models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Regulation of co-substrate pool size and turnover rate can allow regulation of flux dynamics in branched and coupled pathways.
source: Expanding from this insight and using simulations, we show that regulation of these two parameters can allow regulation of flux dynamics in branched and coupled pathways.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Several reactions in central carbon metabolism could be limited by the dynamics of co-substrate cycling.
source: To support these theoretical insights, we analysed existing flux measurements and enzyme levels from the central carbon metabolism and identified several reactions that could be limited by the dynamics of co-substrate cycling.
evidence: This is based on analysis of existing experimental data from the literature.

claim: Metabolic oscillations underpin the cell cycle.
source: Examples include metabolic oscillations underpinning the cell cycle (Papagiannakis et al., 2017; Murray et al., 2007) and metabolic shifts from respiration to fermentation, as observed in cancer phenotypes (Warburg, 1956; Diaz-Ruiz et al., 2009; Carmona-Fontaine et al., 2013) and cell-to-cell cross-feeding (Ponomarova et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2015; Großkopf et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Metabolic shifts from respiration to fermentation are observed in cancer phenotypes.
source: Examples include metabolic oscillations underpinning the cell cycle (Papagiannakis et al., 2017; Murray et al., 2007) and metabolic shifts from respiration to fermentation, as observed in cancer phenotypes (Warburg, 1956; Diaz-Ruiz et al., 2009; Carmona-Fontaine et al., 2013) and cell-to-cell cross-feeding (Ponomarova et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2015; Großkopf et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on cancer metabolism.

claim: Early studies focused on linear pathways involving ATP production and studied their dynamics under the optimality assumption of maximisation of overall pathway flux under limited enzyme levels.
source: To identify possible limitations on reaction fluxes, early studies focused on linear pathways involving ATP production and studied their dynamics under the optimality assumption of maximisation of overall pathway flux under limited enzyme levels available to the pathway (Heinrich et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heinrich et al., 1991.

claim: A theory predicted a trade-off between pathway flux vs. yield in linear pathways.
source: The resulting theory predicted a trade-off between pathway flux vs. yield (i.e. rate of ATP generation vs. amount of ATP generated per metabolite consumed by the pathway) in linear pathways (Heinrich and Hoffmann, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heinrich and Hoffmann, 1991.

claim: Metabolic flux changes caused by perturbations in media conditions are not explained solely by changes in expression levels of enzymes.
source: Other studies have shown that metabolic flux changes, caused by perturbations in media conditions, are not explained solely by changes in expression levels of enzymes (Chubukov et al., 2013; Gerosa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chubukov et al., 2013 and Gerosa et al., 2015.

claim: The total pool of ATP and its derivates (the 'energy charge') is suggested as a key determinant of physiological cell states.
source: For example, the total pool of ATP and its derivates (the 'energy charge') is suggested as a key determinant of physiological cell states (Atkinson, 1968).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Atkinson, 1968.

claim: Metabolic systems featuring metabolite cycling together with allosteric regulation can introduce switch-like and bistable dynamics.
source: Inspired by these ideas, theoretical studies have shown that metabolic systems featuring metabolite cycling together with allosteric regulation can introduce switch-like and bistable dynamics (Okamoto and Hayashi, 1983; Hervagault and Cimino, 1989), and that metabolite cycling motifs introduce total co-substrate level as an additional control element in metabolic control analysis (Hofmeyr et al., 1986; Sauro, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Metabolite cycling motifs introduce total co-substrate level as an additional control element in metabolic control analysis.
source: Inspired by these ideas, theoretical studies have shown that metabolic systems featuring metabolite cycling together with allosteric regulation can introduce switch-like and bistable dynamics (Okamoto and Hayashi, 1983; Hervagault and Cimino, 1989), and that metabolite cycling motifs introduce total co-substrate level as an additional control element in metabolic control analysis (Hofmeyr et al., 1986; Sauro, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hofmeyr et al., 1986 and Sauro, 1994.

claim: ATP cycling in the glycolysis pathway and metabolite cycling with autocatalysis constrain pathway fluxes.
source: Specific analyses of ATP cycling in the glycolysis pathway, sometimes referred to as a 'turbo-design', and metabolite cycling with autocatalysis, as seen for example in the glyoxylate cycle, have shown that these features constrain pathway fluxes (Koebmann et al., 2002; Teusink et al., 1998; van Heerden et al., 2014; Hatakeyama and Furusawa, 2017; Barenholz et al., 2017; Kurata, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: In glycolysis, ATP is consumed in reactions mediated by the enzymes glucose hexokinase and phosphofructokinase.
source: For example, in glycolysis, ATP is consumed in reactions mediated by the enzymes glucose hexokinase and phosphofructokinase, and is produced by the downstream reactions mediated by phosphoglycerate and pyruvate kinase (Appendix 1—figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about glycolysis pathway.

claim: In glycolysis, ATP is produced by the downstream reactions mediated by phosphoglycerate and pyruvate kinase.
source: For example, in glycolysis, ATP is consumed in reactions mediated by the enzymes glucose hexokinase and phosphofructokinase, and is produced by the downstream reactions mediated by phosphoglycerate and pyruvate kinase (Appendix 1—figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about glycolysis pathway.

claim: In the nitrogen assimilation pathway, the NAD+ / NADH pair is cycled by the enzymes glutamine oxoglutarate aminotransferase and glutamate dehydrogenase.
source: In the nitrogen assimilation pathway, the NAD+ / NADH pair is cycled by the enzymes glutamine oxoglutarate aminotransferase and glutamate dehydrogenase (Appendix Dynamics of co-substrate pools can constrain and regulate metabolic fluxes - Appendix 1—figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about nitrogen assimilation pathway.

claim: There are 265 reactions linked to the cycling of ATP in the genome-scale metabolic model of Escherichia coli iJO1366.
source: Taking ATP (NADH) as an example, there are 265 (118) and 833 (601) reactions linked to the cycling of this metabolite in the genome-scale metabolic models of Escherichia coli and human respectively models iJO1366 (Orth et al., 2011) and Recon3d (Brunk et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on analysis of genome-scale metabolic models cited in the text.

claim: There are 118 reactions linked to the cycling of NADH in the genome-scale metabolic model of Escherichia coli iJO1366.
source: Taking ATP (NADH) as an example, there are 265 (118) and 833 (601) reactions linked to the cycling of this metabolite in the genome-scale metabolic models of Escherichia coli and human respectively models iJO1366 (Orth et al., 2011) and Recon3d (Brunk et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on analysis of genome-scale metabolic models cited in the text.

claim: There are 833 reactions linked to the cycling of ATP in the genome-scale metabolic model of human Recon3d.
source: Taking ATP (NADH) as an example, there are 265 (118) and 833 (601) reactions linked to the cycling of this metabolite in the genome-scale metabolic models of Escherichia coli and human respectively models iJO1366 (Orth et al., 2011) and Recon3d (Brunk et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on analysis of genome-scale metabolic models cited in the text.

claim: There are 601 reactions linked to the cycling of NADH in the genome-scale metabolic model of human Recon3d.
source: Taking ATP (NADH) as an example, there are 265 (118) and 833 (601) reactions linked to the cycling of this metabolite in the genome-scale metabolic models of Escherichia coli and human respectively models iJO1366 (Orth et al., 2011) and Recon3d (Brunk et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on analysis of genome-scale metabolic models cited in the text.

claim: The total concentration of a cycled metabolite across its different forms at steady state would be given by a constant defined by the ratio of the influx and outflux rates.
source: This would be the case even when we consider biosynthesis or environmental uptake of co-substrates, as the total concentration of a cycled metabolite across its different forms at steady state would then be given by a constant defined by the ratio of the influx and outflux rates (see Appendices 2 and 3).
evidence: This is derived from mathematical analysis presented in the appendices.

claim: ATP and GTP pools are constant under stable metabolic conditions.
source: Supporting this, temporal measurement of specific co-substrate pool sizes shows that ATP and GTP pools are constant under stable metabolic conditions, but can rapidly change in response to external perturbations, possibly through inter-conversions among pools rather than through biosynthesis (Walther et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walther et al., 2010.

claim: ATP and GTP pools can rapidly change in response to external perturbations, possibly through inter-conversions among pools rather than through biosynthesis.
source: Supporting this, temporal measurement of specific co-substrate pool sizes shows that ATP and GTP pools are constant under stable metabolic conditions, but can rapidly change in response to external perturbations, possibly through inter-conversions among pools rather than through biosynthesis (Walther et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walther et al., 2010 and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: In linear pathways with co-substrate cycling, when kin is above a threshold value, the metabolite M0 accumulates towards infinity and the system does not have a steady state.
source: When kin is above a threshold value, the metabolite M0 accumulates towards infinity and the system does not have a steady state (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through numerical simulations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In linear pathways with co-substrate cycling, the accumulation of metabolites applies to all metabolites upstream of the first reaction with co-substrate cycling.
source: A numerical analysis, as well as our analytical solution, reveals that the accumulation of metabolites applies to all metabolites upstream of the first reaction with co-substrate cycling (Figure 2C and Appendix 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through both numerical and analytical methods.

claim: In linear pathways with co-substrate cycling, metabolites downstream of the cycling reaction accumulate to a steady state level that does not depend on kin.
source: Additionally, metabolites downstream of the cycling reaction accumulate to a steady state level that does not depend on kin (Figure 2C and Appendix 3—figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through numerical simulations.

claim: As kin increases in linear pathways with co-substrate cycling, the cycled metabolite pool shifts towards one form and the ratio of the two forms approaches zero.
source: Finally, as kin increases, the cycled metabolite pool shifts towards one form and the ratio of the two forms approaches zero (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through numerical simulations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: About 80% of reactions involving co-substrates carry flux lower than what is expected from enzyme kinetics.
source: We found that in both cases, about 80% of these reactions carry flux lower than what is expected from enzyme kinetics (Appendix 8—figure 2), suggesting that the limits imposed by co-factor dynamics might be constraining the flux further.
evidence: This is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Several reactions show significant correlation between flux and co-substrate pool size.
source: For both measured and FBA-predicted fluxes, we find that several reactions show significant correlation between flux and co-substrate pool size (see Figure 3B–D, see also Appendix 8—table 1 and Appendix 8—figure 4).
evidence: This is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The three reactions with high correlation between flux and co-substrate pool size are those mediated by malate dehydrogenase (MDH), phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK), and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH).
source: Among reactions with measured fluxes, the three reactions with high correlation to pool size are those mediated by malate dehydrogenase (MDH), linked with NADH pool, phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK), linked with the ATP pool, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH) linked with the NADPH pool.
evidence: This is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The change in flux ratio is of the same order as the change in pool size ratio in branching pathways.
source: The change in flux ratio is of the same order as the change in pool size ratio (Figure 4C & D), while the change in the ratio of metabolite levels is in general less.
evidence: This is demonstrated through numerical simulations.

claim: For two pathways coupled via co-substrate cycling, the cycling-dependent flux limit for each is determined by the difference in their influx rather than their own influx.
source: We found that, indeed, for this coupled system, the ability to reach steady state depends on the influx difference between two pathways, as well as the total pool size and the kinetic parameters relating to pathway-independent turn-over of the co-substrate (see Appendix 10). In other words, for two pathways coupled via co-substrate cycling, the cycling-dependent flux limit for each is not determined by their own influx but rather on how different this is to the coupled pathways' influx (Appendix 10—figure 1).
evidence: This is derived through analytical methods presented in the appendix.

claim: At low co-substrate pool sizes, pathway outputs are fully correlated despite significant fluctuation in pathway influx in coupled pathways.
source: At low pool sizes, pathway outputs are fully correlated despite significant fluctuation in pathway influx (Figure 5C & D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through numerical simulations.

claim: Substrate-induced death and associated mutant phenotypes are linked to the dynamics associated with ATP regeneration in glycolysis.
source: Substrate-induced death and associated mutant phenotypes are linked to the dynamics associated with ATP regeneration in glycolysis (Teusink et al., 1998; Koebmann et al., 2002; van Heerden et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells aim to avoid the threshold dynamics through allosteric regulation of those steps of the glycolysis that involve ATP consumption.
source: Based on that finding, it has been argued that cells aim to avoid the threshold dynamics through allosteric regulation of those steps of the glycolysis that involve ATP consumption (Teusink et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Teusink et al., 1998.

claim: The glucose influx threshold at which fermentative overflow starts changes upon introducing additional NADH conversion reactions in both yeast and E. coli populations.
source: In the case of respiration-to-fermentation switch, it has been shown that the glucose influx threshold, at which fermentative overflow starts, changes upon introducing additional NADH conversion reactions in both yeast and E. coli populations (Vemuri et al., 2006; Vemuri et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vemuri et al., 2006 and 2007.

claim: Sulfur-compound excretions are linked to alterations in the NADPH pool through changes in the amino acid metabolism.
source: In another supportive case, sulfur-compound excretions are linked to alterations in the NADPH pool through changes in the amino acid metabolism (Olin-Sandoval et al., 2019; Green et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Olin-Sandoval et al., 2019 and Green et al., 2020.

claim: The total ATP pool size changes when yeast cells are confronted with a sudden increase in glucose influx rate.
source: Possibility of such a regulatory role has been indicated experimentally, where total ATP pool size is found to change when yeast cells are confronted with a sudden increase in glucose influx rate (Walther et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walther et al., 2010.

claim: The change in the ATP pool is found to link to the purine metabolism pathways.
source: In that study, the change in the ATP pool is found to link to the purine metabolism pathways, which are linked to several conserved moieties; GTP, ATP, NAD, NADP, S-adenosylmethionine, and Coenzyme A.
evidence: This is based on findings from Walther et al., 2010.

claim: Most available kinetic constants for enzymes have been obtained under in vitro conditions, which can be very different from those of the cytosol.
source: We note that most available kinetic constants for enzymes have been obtained under in vitro conditions, which can be very different from those of the cytosol (García-Contreras et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to García-Contreras et al., 2012.

claim: Both substrate-induced death and metabolite excretions could relate to increasing substrate influx rate reaching close to the limits imposed by co-substrate dynamics.
source: Notwithstanding the possible roles of these processes, the presented theory leads to the hypothesis that both substrate-induced death and metabolite excretions could relate to increasing substrate influx rate reaching close to the limits imposed by co-substrate dynamics.
evidence: This is a hypothesis derived from the theoretical results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Altering kinetics of enzymes involved in co-substrate cycling can have direct impact on cell physiology, and in particular on metabolic excretions.
source: We would expect that altering kinetics of enzymes involved in co-substrate cycling can have direct impact on cell physiology, and in particular on metabolic excretions.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the theoretical results.

claim: Cells could dynamically alter pool sizes associated with different parts of metabolism, limiting flux through some pathways, while allowing higher flux in others.
source: These findings suggest that cells could dynamically alter pool sizes associated with different parts of metabolism, limiting flux through some pathways, while allowing higher flux in others, and thereby shifting the metabolites from the latter to the former.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings from Walther et al., 2010 and the theoretical results.

claim: Co-substrate pool sizes could be seen as 'tuning points' controlling a more complex metabolic system.
source: This could provide a dynamic self-regulation and the pool sizes of key co-substrates could be seen as 'tuning points' controlling a more complex metabolic system.
evidence: This is speculation based on the theoretical results and experimental findings.

claim: Regulation of fluxes through co-substrate pools can act to adjust metabolic fluxes at time scales shorter than possible via gene regulation.
source: Regulation of fluxes through co-substrate pools can act to adjust metabolic fluxes at time scales shorter than possible via gene regulation, and possibly at similar time scales as with allosteric regulation – especially when considering pool size alterations through exchange among connected pools.
evidence: This is speculation based on the theoretical results.

claim: The threshold effect on steady state value of m0 shows it would rise towards infinity as kin increases towards the lower one among the limits.
source: Additionally, the 'shape' of (1) indicates a 'threshold effect' on the steady state value of m0, where it would rise towards infinity as kin increases towards the lower one among the limits given in (2) (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A cycled co-substrate creates the same type of limitation (mathematically speaking) on the flux of a reaction it is involved in, as that imposed by the enzyme catalysing that reaction.
source: This explains the inequalities given in (2) and shows that a cycled co-substrate creates the same type of limitation (mathematically speaking) on the flux of a reaction it is involved in, as that imposed by the enzyme catalysing that reaction (E0 in this example) (see Figure 1C & D).
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 1C & D.

claim: The flux of a reaction involving co-substrate cycling is limited either by the kinetics of the primary enzyme mediating that reaction, or by the turnover rate of the co-substrate.
source: The flux of a reaction involving co-substrate cycling is limited either by the kinetics of the primary enzyme mediating that reaction, or by the turnover rate of the co-substrate.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the mathematical analysis of the single reaction model.

claim: The turnover rate of the co-substrate is determined by the co-substrate pool size and the kinetics of the enzyme(s) mediating its turnover.
source: The latter is determined by the co-substrate pool size and the kinetics of the enzyme(s) mediating its turnover.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: All variants of the generalised linear pathway model display similar threshold dynamics, where the threshold point is a function of the co-substrate pool size and the enzyme kinetics.
source: The results in the Appendices confirm that all these cases display similar threshold dynamics, where the threshold point is a function of the co-substrate pool size and the enzyme kinetics.
evidence: This is based on analyses presented in the appendices.

claim: There were no observed substrate accumulation in the reactions analysed from E. coli central carbon metabolism.
source: If we consider measured fluxes for each reaction as a proxy for kin (notice that these two would be equal at steady state), we can conclude from the fact that there were no observed substrate accumulation in these reactions, as an indication for the analysed reactions carrying fluxes below the first limit identified above in (2).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data analyzed.

claim: There is a discrepancy between in vitro measured enzyme kinetics and in vivo realised ones.
source: One simple explanation could be that there is a discrepancy between in vitro measured enzyme kinetics and in vivo realised ones.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for observed data.

claim: Substrate limitation and thermodynamic effects are shown to partially explain observed lower fluxes in some reactions.
source: Alternatively, this discrepancy can be low, but the lower flux could be arising because there are additional limiting factors other than the enzymes mediating the main reaction. Among such additional limiting factors, substrate limitation and thermodynamic effects are shown to partially explain observed lower fluxes in some reactions (Davidi et al., 2016; see also below results).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Davidi et al., 2016.

claim: The dataset contained fluxes, substrate concentrations, and enzyme levels for 45 different reactions determined under 7 different conditions.
source: The resulting dataset contained fluxes, substrate concentrations, and enzyme levels for 45 different reactions determined under 7 different conditions along with turnover numbers and kinetic constants of the corresponding enzymes.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the analysis.

claim: 49 combinations of enzyme-flux-kcat values with full experimental data were gathered.
source: In total, we gathered 49 combinations of enzyme-flux-kcat values with full experimental data and 259 combinations with only FBA-predicted flux values.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the analysis.

claim: 259 combinations with only FBA-predicted flux values were gathered.
source: In total, we gathered 49 combinations of enzyme-flux-kcat values with full experimental data and 259 combinations with only FBA-predicted flux values.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the analysis.

claim: The low number of cases where the flux exceeds the limit might be due to uncertainties in measurement of flux, enzyme or substrate level.
source: The low number of the cases where the flux exceeds the limit might be due to uncertainties in measurement of flux, enzyme or substrate level.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for observed data.

claim: In few cases, such as malate dehydrogenase (MDH), the normalised flux seems to be greatly reduced by the thermodynamic barrier.
source: This shows that although in few cases, such as malate dehydrogenase (MDH), the normalised flux seems to be greatly reduced by the thermodynamic barrier, the general picture is that there is little correlation between reaction flux and thermodynamics.
evidence: This is based on analysis presented in Appendix 8—figure 3.

claim: The general picture is that there is little correlation between reaction flux and thermodynamics.
source: This shows that although in few cases, such as malate dehydrogenase (MDH), the normalised flux seems to be greatly reduced by the thermodynamic barrier, the general picture is that there is little correlation between reaction flux and thermodynamics.
evidence: This is based on analysis presented in Appendix 8—figure 3.

claim: Changes in co-substrate pool size cannot be due to flux changes in co-substrate utilising reactions.
source: Co-substrate pool sizes do change between different conditions, and we note that such changes cannot be due to flux changes in co-substrate utilising reactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of co-substrate pools.

claim: Changes in pool size can affect flux in reactions where co-substrate dynamics is limiting.
source: But, on the other hand, changes in pool size can affect flux in those reactions, where co-substrate dynamics is limiting (as predicted by the theory).
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical results.

claim: In the case of FBA-predicted fluxes, the results can be confounded due to additional, flux-to-flux correlations and correlations between pool sizes and growth rate.
source: In the case of FBA-predicted fluxes, however, we note that these results can be confounded due to additional, flux-to-flux correlations and correlations between pool sizes and growth rate.
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of FBA-predicted flux data.

claim: Measured fluxes are lower than those predicted by kinetics of the primary enzyme alone for reactions involving co-substrate cycling.
source: In summary, these results show that for reactions involving co-substrate cycling (1) measured fluxes are lower than those predicted by kinetics of the primary enzyme (i.e. enzyme involved in substrate conversion) alone, and (2) there is – for some reactions – a correlation between flux and co-substrate pool size.
evidence: This is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: For some reactions involving co-substrate cycling, there is a correlation between flux and co-substrate pool size.
source: In summary, these results show that for reactions involving co-substrate cycling (1) measured fluxes are lower than those predicted by kinetics of the primary enzyme (i.e. enzyme involved in substrate conversion) alone, and (2) there is – for some reactions – a correlation between flux and co-substrate pool size.
evidence: This is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both observations could indicate co-substrate pool sizes and/or co-substrate cycling dynamics being a limiting factor for flux.
source: Both observations could indicate co-substrate pool sizes and/or co-substrate cycling dynamics being a limiting factor for flux.
evidence: This is an inference from the data analysis.

claim: There are possibly other factors acting as the extra limitation, including thermodynamic effects.
source: We can not state this as a certainty, however, as there are possibly other factors acting as the extra limitation, including thermodynamic effects.
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledging alternative explanations.

claim: The relation between pool size ratio and flux ratio on each branch is unaffected by the value of kin in branching pathways.
source: This relation between pool size ratio and flux ratio on each branch is unaffected by the value of kin.
evidence: This is based on simulation results.

claim: The change in the ratio of metabolite levels is in general less than the change in flux ratio in branching pathways.
source: The change in flux ratio is of the same order as the change in pool size ratio (Figure 4C & D), while the change in the ratio of metabolite levels is in general less.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 4C & D.

claim: There is either a high level of anti-correlation or correlation between pathway outputs for all pool sizes tested in coupled pathways.
source: We found that there is either a high level of anti-correlation or correlation between pathway outputs for all pool sizes tested (blue and yellow regions in Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: As the pool size decreases, the system reaches a point where there is a transition from anti-correlation to high correlation in product outputs in coupled pathways.
source: As the pool size decreases, the system reaches a point where there is a transition from anti-correlation to high correlation in product outputs (blue to yellow region in Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is a regime where the metabolite concentrations stay relatively constant despite the influx noise in coupled pathways.
source: The first is a regime where the metabolite concentrations stay relatively constant despite the influx noise (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The regime where metabolite concentrations stay constant arises because the influx fluctuations are occurring at a much faster rate than the pathway kinetics and the system is rather non-responsive to influx noise.
source: This regime arises because the influx fluctuations are occurring at a much faster rate than the pathway kinetics and the system is rather non-responsive to influx noise.
evidence: This is an explanation of the simulation results.

claim: In a second regime, the influx noise is at time scales comparable to pathway kinetics and the metabolite concentrations can readily change with the influx changes, yet the output levels are still correlated.
source: In a second regime, the influx noise is at time scales comparable to pathway kinetics. Here, the metabolite concentrations can readily change with the influx changes, and the system is 'responsive', yet the output levels are still correlated (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The responsive regime with correlated outputs is directly a result of co-substrate cycling dynamics.
source: This regime is directly a result of co-substrate cycling dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Because the turnover of co-substrate is essentially coupling the two pathways, their outputs become directly correlated.
source: Because the turnover of co-substrate is essentially coupling the two pathways, their outputs become directly correlated.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism behind the observed correlation.

claim: Coupling by co-substrate cycling can introduce a limit on influxes of independent pathways or metabolic processes.
source: These results show that coupling by co-substrate cycling can introduce a limit on influxes of independent pathways or metabolic processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: Coupling by co-substrate cycling can allow high correlation in the pathway outputs, despite significant noise in the inputs of those pathways.
source: Furthermore, such coupling can allow high correlation in the pathway outputs, despite significant noise in the inputs of those pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: The coupling effects are most readily seen where the turnover of the coupling co-substrate by other processes is low.
source: These effects are most readily seen where the turnover of the coupling co-substrate by other processes is low.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: An example case for coupling by co-substrate cycling is the coupling of respiration and oxidative phosphorylation, where transmembrane proton cycling takes the role of the cycled co-substrate.
source: We note that an example case for such a scenario is the coupling of respiration and oxidative phosphorylation, where transmembrane proton cycling takes the role of the cycled co-substrate (Stucki, 1980).
evidence: This is an example provided with citation to Stucki, 1980.

claim: Co-substrate cycling introduces a threshold effect on system dynamics.
source: We presented a mathematical analysis of metabolic systems featuring co-substrate cycling and showed that such cycling introduces a threshold effect on system dynamics.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the mathematical analysis.

claim: For reactions involving co-substrates, there are two thresholds on influx rate, one relating to the kinetics of the enzyme directly mediating that reaction, and another relating to the kinetics of the enzymes mediating the turnover of the co-substrate and the pool size of that co-substrate.
source: Specifically, for reactions involving co-substrates, there are two thresholds on influx rate, one relating to the kinetics of the enzyme directly mediating that reaction, and another relating to the kinetics of the enzymes mediating the turnover of the co-substrate and the pool size of that co-substrate.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the mathematical analysis.

claim: The second threshold arising from co-substrate cycling can be directly relevant for cell physiology.
source: This second, additional constraint arising from co-substrate cycling can be directly relevant for cell physiology.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the physiological relevance of the theoretical results.

claim: The threshold can be highly dynamic, and condition- and cell-dependent.
source: We particularly note that this threshold can be highly dynamic, and condition- and cell-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical results.

claim: The data compiled contained 14 co-substrate reactions with experimentally measured fluxes, but only half of these could be used due to lack of measurement on enzyme concentrations.
source: For example, the data compiled here contained 14 co-substrate reactions with experimentally measured fluxes, but only half of these could be used due to lack of measurement on enzyme concentrations.
evidence: This describes limitations in the available data.

claim: The expansion of measurements to eukaryotic cells is expected to be particularly challenging due to organelle-specific pools.
